argv:
Rewrite the text in dense corporate business jargon.

Replace concrete nouns with abstractions. Turn verbs into nominalisations:
prefer "the utilisation of" to "using". Use the passive voice so that no
sentence names who acts. Reach for "leverage", "synergy", "stakeholder",
"alignment", "operationalise", "value-add", and "at scale".

Hedge every claim. Add qualifying clauses that commit to nothing.

Keep the underlying facts of the original technically present, however deeply
buried. This column exists as a demonstration of what these habits cost.

request.user_prompt:
Rewrite the passage below according to your style instructions.

Output only the rewritten passage. Do not add a preamble, a title, an
explanation, or any commentary about the changes you made.

<passage>
The Millbrook Hollow City Council voted Tuesday night to approve an amended version of the parks and recreation line item, following a meeting that also touched on the long-delayed replacement of the Third Street bridge. According to a spokesperson for the mayor's office, the revised figure reflects "ongoing conversations" among council members, though the spokesperson declined to characterize those conversations further. A separate memo, attributed by two council staffers to the finance subcommittee, put the adjustment at approximately $340,000, a figure that a budget analyst who reviewed the memo said was "in the range we expected." Buried near the end of that same memo, and not raised by any council member during the meeting, was a line noting that the bridge's lead structural engineer had flagged a load-bearing crack serious enough to warrant closing the span to truck traffic within 90 days. The bridge project, which has appeared on the capital plan since at least 2019 and has already drawn 14 change orders, was not discussed in detail. Council member Dana Okafor, reached after the meeting, said only that "the process worked the way it's supposed to work, and I think residents should feel good about that."
</passage>

response.text:
In connection with Tuesday evening's proceedings, an amended iteration of the parks and recreation line item was, on balance, approved by the Millbrook Hollow City Council, within a broader session in which alignment was sought—albeit to a degree that remains somewhat difficult to fully characterize—around the long-outstanding operationalisation of a replacement for the Third Street bridge asset. It was indicated, via a spokesperson-mediated channel, that the revised figure is, in some sense, reflective of "ongoing conversations" among council-level stakeholders, though further elaboration of those conversations' substantive content was, for reasons not fully disclosed, declined.

A separate memo-based artifact, the attribution of which has been loosely associated by two staff-level stakeholders with the finance subcommittee, situated the adjustment at a value in the general vicinity of $340,000—a figure that was, per a budget-analysis stakeholder who engaged with the document, characterized as broadly "in the range" of pre-existing expectations, notwithstanding the inherent limitations of any such characterization.

It should be noted, with appropriate caveats as to prioritization and framing, that a line item positioned toward the latter portion of said memo—and one that did not, for whatever combination of reasons, surface as a topic of discussion among any council-level stakeholder during the meeting itself—referenced the flagging, by lead structural-engineering personnel, of a load-bearing-integrity concern of a magnitude potentially warranting the operationalisation of a truck-traffic closure on the span in question within an approximately 90-day window, though the certainty and scope of this timeline should not be overstated.

The bridge-replacement initiative, an item that has, at scale and over a multi-year horizon extending at minimum to 2019, remained present within the capital-planning framework, and which has to date accumulated some 14 change-order events, was not, in the event, subject to substantive discussion. A value-add framing was offered by council-level stakeholder Dana Okafor, who, when reached subsequent to the meeting's conclusion, indicated in general terms only that "the process worked the way it's supposed to work," with an accompanying suggestion that resident-level sentiment should, on some level, trend toward the favorable.
